rationale: A wins because it keeps the sharpest story grounded: "Instacart Built Its Brand on Grocery Delivery. Its Advertising Business Just Hit $1 Billion" is a real business-model angle with the right proof burden attached. B is punchier, but "A cart that watches what you put in it is now the grocery aisle's newest ad surface" states the unproven part as fact, then tries to clean it up in the proof list. That is how founders get walked into a reporter's follow-up they cannot answer.
gaps_in_A: "with a stated plan to grow across 1,500+ banner partners" overreads the update. The facts say Instacart has 1,500+ retail banners and smart carts have plans to expand, not that carts are expanding across that whole partner base.
"as digital attribution has gotten harder" is an imported macro trend. It may be true, but it was not in the update and needs outside evidence before it carries an angle.

"$1B in Ad Revenue" is looser than the supplied fact, which says a "$1B annual run rate" for the advertising business. A reporter will ask whether that is recognized revenue, gross bookings, or annualized quarter math.
gaps_in_B: "is now the grocery aisle's newest ad surface" is the big sin. The update says Caper carts track items and Instacart has ads; it does not say carts carry ads, feed targeting, or create in-store inventory.
"the vast majority of banners have not deployed them" is bad arithmetic. The update gives store count and banner count, which are not interchangeable units.
"this beat has already seen fail twice" is invented color. No prior failed smart-cart or cashierless-store examples were supplied.

"The prevailing belief in retail media is that ad revenue rides on top of a growing transaction base" may be a smart thesis, but it is not in the provided facts and needs sourcing before it becomes the spine of the pitch.
